issue.close_reason:
Root cause identified: Zone minimum radius too large for 2-player mode

## Root Cause (Option A): Zone minimum radius is too large

Current: ZoneMinRadius = 2 for 2-player (diameter = 4 tiles)
Expected: ZoneMinRadius = 1 for 2-player (diameter = 2 tiles)

## Supporting Evidence from Replay:

✓ Combat IS executing: Turn 13 shows combat_death events
✓ Bots ARE reaching same area: Positions (17,19) and (14,22), distance ≈ 4.2 tiles  
✓ Damage IS being dealt: 1v1 mutual destruction (both died)
✓ Zone IS shrinking: Radius 18→15 over turns 10-13

Critical finding: At turn 13 when combat occurred:
- Zone radius: 15 (diameter 30) - still very large
- Bot distance: 4.2 tiles (within 5-tile attack radius)  
- Combat happened because bots chose to move together, NOT because zone forced them

## Code Path Responsible:

File: engine/types.go, line 250
Function: ConfigForPlayers()  
Specific line: cfg.ZoneMinRadius = 2 // Per plan §3.7.1: 2-player min radius

Current config creates zone diameter 4 (radius 2), allowing bots to stay 4 tiles apart at opposite edges - barely within 5-tile attack radius.

## Recommended Fix:

Change cfg.ZoneMinRadius from 2 to 1 for 2-player mode (engine/types.go:250).

This creates zone diameter 2, matching 3+ player mode and forcing bots within attack radius (5 > 2).

issue.notes:
Pipeline architecture verified from code:

## Matchmaker → Worker → Engine → B2/R2 Upload → Index Build

**Phase 1 - Matchmaker (cmd/acb-matchmaker/tickers.go)**
- Runs tickMatchmaker() every 60s
- Implements sophisticated pairing: seed=oldest last-match, format=least-played player count, opponents=Pareto skill-proximity + recency
- Creates match/participant/job records in PostgreSQL
- Enqueues job ID to Valkey (LPUSH to acb:jobs:pending)
- ALSO health-checks bots (every 900s) and reaps stale jobs (every 300s)

**Phase 2 - Worker (cmd/acb-worker/main.go + db.go)**
- Polls PostgreSQL every 5s: GetNextJob() with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
- Claims job atomically: ClaimJob() updates status='claimed', sets worker_id
- Executes match via engine with HTTP bot communication
- Uploads replay to B2 (via ARMOR) AND R2 (direct hot cache)
- Writes results + Glicko-2 ratings to PostgreSQL
- Updates live feeds: live-tail.json, live-delta.json

**Phase 3 - Engine (engine/match.go + game.go)**
- Runs match turn-by-turn with bot HTTP calls
- Records replay with events and telemetry
- Returns MatchResult + Replay

**Phase 4 - Index Builder (cmd/acb-index-builder/main.go)**
- Runs continuous build cycles (every 60s in-cluster: 15m build interval)
- fetchAllData() from PostgreSQL: bots, matches, ratings, series, seasons, predictions, maps, feedback, evolution metadata
- generateAllIndexes(): static JSON files (bots/index.json, matches/index.json, series/index.json, seasons/index.json, meta/archetypes.json, meta/rivalries.json, evolution/meta.json, evolution/lineage.json)
- bundleWarmAssetsForCycle(): downloads recent replays from B2, bundles into Pages deploy
- uploadMetaJSONToR2(): uploads static files to R2 warm cache
- deployToPages(): deploys to Cloudflare Pages every N cycles (6 cycles = ~90m)

**Deployment Configuration Verified (manifests/*.yml):**
- Worker: 2 replicas, polls PostgreSQL every 5s, B2 endpoint=http://armor:9000, R2 credentials from secret
- Matchmaker: 1 replica, runs every 60s, connects to PostgreSQL + Valkey
- Index Builder: 1 replica, 15m build interval, R2 + B2 credentials from secret

## Blockers
Cannot verify live runtime - kubectl credentials expired (iad-kalshi OIDC token ~3 day expiry). ArgoCD sync may be working but pod/logs inaccessible without fresh admin token.

## What To Check Next

2. Check pod status: kubectl get pods -n ai-code-battle
3. Check matchmaker logs for job creation: kubectl logs -l app=acb-matchmaker --tail=50
4. Check worker logs for match execution: kubectl logs -l app=acb-worker --tail=50
5. Query B2 bucket for replay files: ls -la replays/

issue.description:
docs/plan/plan.md section 7.1 documents delta encoding as an intended
optimization for the turns array on long matches ("for very long matches,
the turns array can use delta encoding -- only recording events that
changed from the previous turn") but this is not implemented: engine/replay.go
has no delta logic (grepped for "delta"/"Delta" in engine/replay.go --
only hit is an unrelated Direction.Delta() helper in engine/types.go).
Every turn in a replay is currently stored in full.

Each turn already only records deltas conceptually (moves, spawns,
deaths, captures, energy_collected, energy_spawned, scores -- see the
example schema in section 7.1) rather than full grid state, so the "delta
encoding" here specifically means: don't re-emit unchanged per-player
score/energy totals every turn if they didn't change since the last turn,
and consider omitting turns array entries for structurally uneventful
turns (dedupeable via the existing gzip pass, but true delta encoding
reduces pre-gzip size and, more importantly, parse/reconstruction time in
web/src/lib/replay-data.ts on load).

Concrete scope: measure current uncompressed/gzipped replay size for a
representative 500-turn 4-player match (section 7.1 estimates
200-500KB / 30-80KB), implement delta encoding for the turns array in
engine/replay.go, update the replay format version, update
web/src/lib/replay-data.ts to reconstruct full per-turn state from deltas,
and confirm the replay viewer (web/src/replay-viewer.ts) still renders
identically. Bump replay schema version and update
web/public/replay-schema-v1.json (or introduce v2) accordingly.

Value: smaller payload = faster replay-viewer first paint, especially on
mobile/slow connections, which is the primary way visitors experience
this platform (section 7.3).

issue.close_reason: Verified the ACB SHA parameter fix is already deployed and healthy: argoWorkflow-level body.after mappings are present on both ACB sensors, all semantic checks pass, and the live sensor is Ready with DependenciesProvided/Deployed/TriggersProvided=True. No duplicate source change required.
issue.description:
All four ACB WorkflowTemplates failed on iad-ci on 2026-08-06, twice each
(runs ~94m and ~99m apart). Observed 2026-08-06 12:35Z.

| workflow | failing node | exit |
|---|---|---|
| acb-build-dqhxq / -fv7fs | build-api, build-worker, build-enrichment, build-evolver, build-map-evolver, build-matchmaker, build-index-builder — all 7 | 1 |
| acb-enrichment-build-lp6x4 / -swt79 | docker-build | 1 |
| acb-images-build-np4cs / -s4b8n | test | 128 |
| acb-site-pages-build-q2h78 / -sfmwc | 4 retries, "No more retries left" | 128 |

## Likely root cause: the sensor is not expanding the commit SHA

Every failed run carries its `commit-sha` parameter as the **literal
unexpanded string**:

    commit-sha = {{dependencies.acb-push.body.after}}

That is the Argo Events trigger template, not a SHA. A `git checkout` of
that literal ref fails with **exit 128**, which is exactly what
acb-images-build (`test`) and acb-site-pages-build report. The exit-1
failures in acb-build/acb-enrichment are plausibly the same checkout
failure surfacing later in the build.

`acb-build.yml` declares the parameter as `sha` with the comment "Short
commit SHA, supplied by the Argo Events sensor", while the submitted
workflows pass `commit-sha`. Worth checking whether the sensor and the
template disagree on the parameter name — that would leave `sha` unset and
`commit-sha` unexpanded, matching what we see.

## Where to look

- `declarative-config/k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/acb-eventsensor.yml` —
  the `acb-push` dependency and its `dataTemplate`/parameter wiring
- `declarative-config/k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/acb-build.yml` —
  parameter named `sha`, no default
- repo: `git.ardenone.com/jedarden/ai-code-battle`

## Reproducing

Pod logs are gone (`podGC: OnPodCompletion`). To capture them, resubmit with
a `podGC: OnWorkflowCompletion` override, or stream while running.

Note: these ran while iad-ci could not schedule new pods (see the capacity
bead in declarative-config), so confirm the failures are independent of that.
issue.notes: Verified already shipped in declarative-config main; no additional file changes needed. Current sensor manifests use argoWorkflow.parameters (not trigger-level parameters) with dataKey body.after mapped to spec.arguments.parameters.0.value, and use the fail-closed sensor-must-supply-commit-sha placeholder. Live iad-ci inspection: Forgejo and GitHub ACB Sensors both report DependenciesProvided=True, Deployed=True, TriggersProvided=True; sensor pod Ready; referenced ACB WorkflowTemplates exist. Static YAML/semantic assertions pass for both sensors and ACB templates. ./k8s/check-resource-limits.py iad-ci reports 271 files checked, 0 critical findings (pre-existing low findings only). ArgoCD argo-events-ns-iad-ci and argo-workflows-iad-ci are Synced/Healthy at 0f210419. No source commit made because the fix was already present (017b2e71/6fb56090); the old exit-128 runs are historical and pod/workflow records are GC'd.

Two features already exist independently but aren't connected:

- Win probability + critical moments (docs/plan/plan.md section 13.2,
  engine/winprob.go ComputeWinProbability): each replay stores a
  critical_moments array (turn, delta, description) for turns where win
  probability shifted >15%.
- Clip maker (web/src/pages/clip-maker.ts): lets a user pick a replay,
  scrub to a start/end turn, and export MP4/GIF in 5 social presets.
  Grepped clip-maker.ts for "critical_moment"/"criticalMoment" -- no hits,
  confirming it's not reading the field at all today.

Currently a user has to already know (or manually scrub to find) the
interesting moment in a match before they can clip it. Wire
clip-maker.ts to read the replay's critical_moments array (already fetched
as part of the replay JSON) and offer one-click "jump to critical moment
N" buttons that set the clip start/end range around that turn (e.g.
critical_moment.turn +/- ~15 turns), the same way the replay viewer's
win-probability graph already supports "click to jump" / "next critical
moment" per section 13.2.

Value: turns "watch a 5-minute replay to find the good part" into "click
the pre-flagged highlight, export it" -- directly serves the platform's
own stated shareability goal (section 13's clip-maker, embed.html,
og-tags.ts) with near-zero new backend work since the data already
exists in the replay.

issue.notes:
## False Positive Starvation Alert - Root Cause Analysis (2026-08-29)

### Finding
This is a **false positive starvation alert** caused by checkpoint/database desynchronization, not actual worker starvation.

### Root Cause: Checkpoint Metadata Mismatch

**Checkpoint (current.json) claims:**
- issue_count: 130
- total_record_count: 1121
- Dependency graph: 46 blocked issues

**Live database actually contains:**
- 100 beads (ALL closed)
- 0 open beads
- 0 in_progress beads

**Missing:** 30 beads that checkpoint believes exist but are not visible in the database.

### Evidence
1. `bead list --json | jq -s 'length'` → 100 (all status: closed)
2. `bead doctor` → "Schema validity OK: 130 issues validated" (reads checkpoint)
3. `bead list --ready` → "No issues found" (correct - no open beads)
4. `bead list --status open` → [] (empty - no open beads)

### Why Pluck Triggers the Alert
Pluck reads checkpoint metadata (130 issues, 46 blocked) and expects work to exist, but when querying the database for claimable beads, it finds none (all 100 are closed). This mismatch causes the starvation detector to fire.

### Correct Behavior
The system is functioning correctly - there are genuinely 0 open beads available to claim. The starvation alert is caused by stale checkpoint metadata, not an actual worker starvation problem.

### Recommended Fix
Sync checkpoint to match live database state:
```
bead sync flush-only
```
This will republish the checkpoint with the correct issue count (100, not 130).

issue.notes:
## acb-bots-build Workflow Analysis Complete

### Workflow Structure
**Location:** declarative-config/k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/acb-bots-build-workflowtemplate.yml

**Purpose:** Build all 21 AI Code Battle strategy bot images and push to Docker Hub

### Key Design Features
1. **Concurrency Control:** parallelism: 3 (caps simultaneous builds to prevent cluster overload)
   - Without this cap, all 21 builds would request 21 CPU / 42Gi simultaneously
   - iad-ci cluster has only 15.00 CPU / 26.08Gi total allocatable
   - Fixed scheduling starvation and OOM failures from previous unbounded runs

2. **Build Tool:** Kaniko executor v1.23.2 (Google Container Registry image)
   - Builds directly from git context without local Docker daemon
   - Supports layer caching via ronaldraygun/cache repository

3. **Authentication:** Forgejo webhook token (secret: forgejo-webhook-token)
   - Used for git clone and Kaniko git context access
   - Docker Hub credentials from docker-hub-registry secret

### All 21 Bot Images Built
1. assassin
2. coordinator  
3. defender
4. economist
5. farmer
6. gatherer
7. guardian
8. hunter
9. kamikaze
10. leader-targeter

12. opportunist
13. pacifist
14. phalanx
15. raider
16. random
17. rusher
18. scout
19. siege
20. swarm
21. zone-driver

### Docker Hub Push Mechanism
Each bot image produces **4 tags**:
- ronaldraygun/acb-bot-{name}:sha-{sha}
- ronaldraygun/acb-strategy-{name}:sha-{sha}
- ronaldraygun/acb-bot-{name}:latest
- ronaldraygun/acb-strategy-{name}:latest

The dual naming (both acb-bot-* and acb-strategy-*) supports different use cases in the codebase.

### Resource Limits per Build
- Requests: 1000m CPU / 2Gi memory
- Limits: 1500m CPU / 4Gi memory
- Active deadline: 1800s (30 minutes)
- Retry strategy: 2 attempts with exponential backoff (30s, 60s)

### Dependent Workflow Templates

**1. acb-images-build** (declarative-config/k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/acb-images-build-workflowtemplate.yml)
- Builds core ACB service images: matchmaker, worker, index-builder, api, evolver, enrichment
- Also builds some strategy bots: random, gatherer, rusher, guardian, swarm, hunter
- Pushes to **Forgejo container registry** (forgejo.ardenone.com/ai-code-battle/*)
- Uses DAG structure with test dependency before builds
- Runs Go tests + web type-check/lint before building

**2. acb-build** (declarative-config/k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/acb-build-workflowtemplate.yml)
- Builds different core services: matchmaker, worker, index-builder, api, evolver, map-evolver, enrichment
- Pushes to **Docker Hub** (ronaldraygun/*)
- Includes **update-declarative-config step** that resolves Docker Hub digests and commits image updates to declarative-config repo
- Runs Go tests + web type-check/lint before building

### Workflow Relationships
- **acb-bots-build**: Bot strategy images → Docker Hub (ronaldraygun/acb-bot-*, acb-strategy-*)
- **acb-images-build**: Core services + some bots → Forgejo registry (internal)
- **acb-build**: Core services → Docker Hub + auto-updates declarative-config

The three workflows serve different purposes:
- acb-bots-build: All 21 public strategy bots for external use
- acb-images-build: Internal registry builds for Forgejo-hosted infrastructure
- acb-build: Core services with GitOps automation for deployment manifests

issue.description:
The in-browser WASM sandbox (web/src/pages/sandbox.ts, wasm/) currently
ships only 6 opponent bots: gatherer, rusher, swarm, random, guardian,
hunter (see wasm/Makefile and buildOpponentRow in sandbox.ts). guardian
and hunter are deliberate Go reimplementations of the PHP/Java originals
per docs/plan/plan.md section 13.1 (PHP/Java aren't WASM-practical) -- that
part is correct and should stay as-is.

But per the plan's own language-compatibility table (section 13.1), Go,
Rust, and TypeScript are all "Full" WASM support, and bots/ has 12 more
strategy bots in those languages that are NOT yet in the sandbox:
assassin, phalanx, zone-driver (Rust); coordinator (TypeScript);
economist, farmer, opportunist, siege (Go); plus defender (C#, not
WASM-practical, skip), and kamikaze/pacifist/leader-targeter/nomad/
raider/scout in Java/JS/Python (lower priority -- JS ones ARE
WASM-practical via existing swarm.js pattern, Python needs Pyodide per
section 13.1 and is a separate, heavier lift).

Concrete scope for this bead: add WASM builds + sandbox opponent-select
entries for the 4 Go bots (economist, farmer, opportunist, siege) and 3
Rust bots (assassin, phalanx, zone-driver) using the existing build.sh /
wasm-pack patterns in wasm/bots/{gatherer,rusher}. This takes the sandbox
from 6 to 13 opponents without touching the JS/Python/C# tier, which is a
separate follow-on if wanted.

Value: the sandbox (docs/plan/plan.md section 13.1) is the platform's
zero-deployment onboarding path -- more opponent variety directly
increases how much of the real strategic diversity a newcomer can
practice against before committing to the HTTP ladder.

issue.description:
Rename the default branch from `master` to `main` to match the convention
used by every other repo in the workspace.

No force-push is involved: this creates a new ref at the same commit, not
a history rewrite.

## Repo-side surfaces

| surface | current | how |
|---|---|---|
| Forgejo default branch | `master` | `PATCH /api/v1/repos/jedarden/ai-code-battle` `{"default_branch":"main"}` (branch must exist first) |
| GitHub mirror default | `master` (only branch) | `gh api -X PATCH repos/jedarden/ai-code-battle -f default_branch=main` — only after the push mirror has carried `main` across |
| Cloudflare Pages production branch | `master` | **Cloudflare dashboard only** — not in the repo. See `web/CLOUDFLARE_DEPLOYMENT.md` |
| local clone (ex44) | `master` | `git branch -m master main` + reset upstream |

Docs to update (historical `notes/bf-*.md` deliberately excluded — they
record what was true at the time and should not be rewritten):

- `PROGRESS.md:58,165`
- `DEPLOYMENT_STEPS.md:65`
- `web/CLOUDFLARE_DEPLOYMENT.md:14,19`
- `web/DEPLOYMENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md:77`

- No branch protection rules on Forgejo
- No open pull requests
- **No ArgoCD Application tracks this repo** — ArgoCD tracks
  declarative-config only, so there is no GitOps sync impact
- No clone on the lab server; ex44 is the only working copy
- `.github/workflows/*.disabled` — GH Actions stay disabled
- The Forgejo webhook fires on all pushes; branch filtering is done by the
  sensor, so the webhook itself needs no change

## Cross-repo ordering

The CI-side changes live in declarative-config and bracket this bead:

1. declarative-config **bf-637** — sensors accept both refs (before)
2. **this bead** — rename, defaults, external settings, docs
3. declarative-config **bf-2sg** — template defaults -> `main`, then drop
   `master` from the sensor filters after a soak

Cloudflare Pages is the one surface with no automation path; if its
production branch is not updated, production deploys silently become
preview deploys. Check bf-414 first — it may move Pages onto Argo
`acb-site-build`, which would remove this surface entirely.

Blocked on bf-1dla (sensor passes `commit-sha` as an unexpanded
`{{dependencies.acb-push.body.after}}`, exit-128 checkouts) and on
declarative-config bf-37c (iad-ci cannot schedule pods at all). Renaming
now adds a third variable to a system that cannot currently produce a
green build, so a failure afterwards could not be attributed.

dead stub types/functions from deploy.go, keep the real implementations in
s3.go/cards.go, add the missing R2Object type and Config.PagesProject

Drafted complete updated section 5 content for plan.md:

## 5. Strategy Bots

Twenty-one built-in strategy bots serve as reference implementations and permanent
ladder opponents. These demonstrate a wide range of strategies across multiple
programming languages, showing that the HTTP protocol is language-agnostic and
providing diverse opponents for competition.

Each bot is deployed as its own container running a lightweight HTTP server.

| Bot | Language | Strategy | Expected Rank |
|-----|----------|----------|---------------|
| RandomBot | Python | Random valid moves — baseline reference | 21st (floor) |
| GathererBot | Go | Energy collection priority, avoids combat | 15th–18th |
| RusherBot | Rust | Rushes enemy cores aggressively | 14th–17th |
| GuardianBot | PHP | Defends cores, cautious expansion | 13th–16th |
| SwarmBot | TypeScript | Formation cohesion, advances as a group | 5th–8th |
| HunterBot | Java | Targets isolated enemy units | 4th–7th |
| AssassinBot | Rust | Decapitation: all units rush enemy core | 8th–11th |
| CoordinatorBot | TypeScript | Dynamic role allocation (Attacker/Harvester/Defender/Scout) | 3rd–6th |
| DefenderBot | C# | Pure defensive posture, core perimeter defense | 12th–15th |
| EconomistBot | Python | Energy starvation through node contesting | 10th–13th |
| FarmerBot | Go | Long-term energy farming strategy | 11th–14th |
| KamikazeBot | JavaScript | Sacrificial rush tactics | 16th–19th |
| LeaderTargeterBot | Java | Focuses fire on the strongest opponent | 6th–9th |
| NomadBot | Python | Constant relocation, mobile skirmishing | 9th–12th |
| OpportunistBot | Go | Exploits momentary advantages | 7th–10th |
| PacifistBot | JavaScript | Avoids combat entirely | 19th–21st |
| PhalanxBot | Rust | Tight defensive formation, maximizes local firepower | 5th–8th |
| RaiderBot | Java | Hit-and-run energy denial | 8th–11th |
| ScoutBot | Python | Prioritizes map exploration and vision control | 13th–16th |
| SiegeBot | Go | Blocks enemy core spawning by surrounding cores | 4th–7th |
| ZoneDriverBot | Rust | Weaponizes shrinking zone to force eliminations | 2nd–5th |

### 5.1 Bot Implementations

**Language distribution:** Strategy bots demonstrate true language-agnostic HTTP protocol design across 8 programming languages:

- **Go (4 bots):** farmer, gatherer, opportunist, siege
- **Rust (4 bots):** assassin, phalanx, rusher, zone-driver
- **Python (4 bots):** economist, nomad, random, scout
- **Java (3 bots):** hunter, leader-targeter, raider
- **TypeScript (2 bots):** coordinator, swarm
- **JavaScript (2 bots):** kamikaze, pacifist
- **PHP (1 bot):** guardian
- **C# (1 bot):** defender

This distribution shows that the HTTP protocol works across all major language families while maintaining diversity in implementation approaches.

**Implementation patterns:**
- All bots implement the same HTTP contract: POST /turn (game state → moves) and GET /health (liveness)
- HMAC verification using language-standard crypto libraries
- Game state parsing and move generation logic varies by language idioms
- Each bot maintains its own strategy-specific state across turns

### 5.2 Reference Bot Descriptions

#### RandomBot (Python)
The simplest possible bot — makes uniformly random valid moves. Serves as the baseline reference; any competent bot should beat it. Pure random-move strategy provides a floor for competitive ranking.

#### Core Strategy Bots
These demonstrate fundamental strategic concepts:

- **GathererBot (Go):** BFS to nearest energy, avoids combat entirely. Tests whether passive resource collection can outpace aggression.
- **RusherBot (Rust):** Rushes enemy cores aggressively using BFS pathfinding. Ignores energy and enemy bots unless they block the path. Punishes bots that neglect defense.
- **GuardianBot (PHP):** Defends cores with cautious expansion. Maintains defensive perimeter and tests turtling viability.
- **SwarmBot (TypeScript):** Maintains formation cohesion (units stay grouped), advances as a coordinated force. Exploits focus-fire combat mechanics through local superiority.
- **HunterBot (Java):** Targets isolated enemy units (≥4 tiles from nearest friendly), sends pairs for 2v1 kills. Sophisticated target selection with tactical awareness.

#### Advanced Strategy Bots
These demonstrate more sophisticated tactics and role specialization:

- **AssassinBot (Rust):** Decapitation archetype — all units rush the enemy core, ignoring enemy units and economy. Commits fully to core destruction with no perimeter defense.
- **CoordinatorBot (TypeScript):** Dynamic role allocation strategy. Each turn assigns each bot a role (Attacker/Harvester/Defender/Scout) and coordinates actions across the entire field.
- **DefenderBot (C#):** Core-defense archetype. Bots stay within N cells of their own core, intercepting any enemy unit that enters the perimeter. Pure defensive posture.
- **EconomistBot (Python):** Energy starvation through node contesting. Deliberately contests energy nodes that enemies are approaching, denying opponent economy while building advantage.
- **FarmerBot (Go):** Long-term energy farming with map control. Sustainable economic strategy over aggression.
- **KamikazeBot (JavaScript):** Sacrificial rush tactics. Trades units efficiently for map control and disruption.
- **LeaderTargeterBot (Java):** Focuses fire on the strongest opponent (highest-rated bot). Anti-leader strategy targeted at top of ladder.
- **NomadBot (Python):** Constant relocation archetype. Mobile skirmishing that avoids prolonged engagements, rarely stays in one area.
- **OpportunistBot (Go):** Exploits momentary advantages and opponent mistakes. Reactive strategy that capitalizes on tactical errors.
- **PacifistBot (JavaScript):** Avoids combat entirely. Tests pure economic victory potential without military engagement.
- **PhalanxBot (Rust):** Tight formation archetype. All units move as a coordinated group, maximizing local firepower at the cost of map coverage.
- **RaiderBot (Java):** Hit-and-run energy denial tactics. Disrupts opponent economy while avoiding decisive engagement.
- **ScoutBot (Python):** Prioritizes map exploration and vision control. Information-gathering strategy for positional advantage.
- **SiegeBot (Go):** Blocks enemy core spawning by surrounding cores. Positional denial that prevents opponent reinforcements.
- **ZoneDriverBot (Rust):** Weaponizes the shrinking zone to force eliminations. Computes zone boundary, identifies the kill band, and positions units to block enemy escape routes. Turns the zone from map feature into active weapon.

### 5.3 Value as Reference Implementations

These bots serve multiple purposes:

1. **Opponents for testing:** New bot developers have a range of strategies to test against before competitive deployment.
2. **Code examples:** Each bot demonstrates a complete, working HTTP bot implementation with HMAC authentication in its language.
3. **Strategy benchmarks:** The rating distribution shows which strategic approaches are effective in the current meta.
4. **Meta diversity:** Different playstyles ensure no single strategy dominates the ladder.

### 5.4 Container Templates

Each bot uses a language-appropriate container structure. All share the same contract: listen on port 8080, serve POST /turn and GET /health.

**Language-specific structures:**

```
bots/{bot-name}/
├── Dockerfile
├── main.{go,py,rs,ts,php,java,js,cs}  # HTTP server, HMAC verification
├── strategy.{go,py,rs,ts,php,java,js,cs}  # Bot-specific strategy logic (if separated)
├── game/                               # Game state types and grid utilities (varies by language)
└── {go.mod,Cargo.toml,package.json,requirements.txt,pom.xml,bundler.csproj}  # Language-specific deps
```

**Shared contract (all bots):**
- Listen on port 8080
- POST /turn — receives game state, runs strategy, returns moves
- GET /health — returns 200 (used for registration health check)
- HMAC signature verification on incoming requests
- HMAC signature on outgoing responses
- Request logging (turn number, compute time, move count)

**Container specs:**

| Language | Base Image | Memory Limit | CPU Limit |
|----------|------------|-------------|-----------|
| Python (4 bots) | python:3.13-slim | 64MB | 0.1 cores |
| Go (4 bots) | golang:1.24-alpine → alpine:3.21 | 128MB | 0.25 cores |
| Rust (4 bots) | rust:1.83-alpine → alpine:3.21 | 128MB | 0.25 cores |
| Java (3 bots) | eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine | 192MB | 0.3 cores |
| TypeScript (2 bots) | node:22-alpine → alpine:3.21 | 128MB | 0.25 cores |
| JavaScript (2 bots) | node:22-alpine → alpine:3.21 | 96MB | 0.2 cores |
| PHP (1 bot) | php:8.4-cli-alpine | 96MB | 0.2 cores |
| C# (1 bot) | mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:9.0-alpine | 128MB | 0.25 cores |

All bots are intentionally lightweight — strategy bots should focus on algorithmic efficiency, not resource consumption.

### 5.5 Starter Kit & SDK Libraries

To lower the barrier for participants writing their own bots, the platform provides starter kits for each supported language. Each starter kit is a minimal, forkable repository containing:

- A working HTTP server with HMAC verification already implemented
- Type definitions for the game state and move schemas
- Grid utility functions (toroidal distance, BFS, neighbor enumeration)
- A stub strategy function that holds all bots in place (participant fills in)
- A Dockerfile that builds and runs the bot
- A README with quickstart instructions

**Starter kit languages (matching strategy bots):**

| Kit | Repository | Notes |
|-----|-----------|-------|
| acb-starter-python | Template repo | Flask-based, ~100 lines total |
| acb-starter-go | Template repo | Shares game/ package with GathererBot |
| acb-starter-rust | Template repo | axum + serde, strongly typed |
| acb-starter-php | Template repo | Zero dependencies, built-in server |
| acb-starter-typescript | Template repo | Fastify, full type definitions |
| acb-starter-java | Template repo | Javalin, Maven-based |
| acb-starter-javascript | Template repo | Node.js built-in http, zero dependencies |
| acb-starter-csharp | Template repo | ASP.NET Core minimal API, zero external dependencies |

Participants are not limited to these languages. Any language that can serve HTTP and compute HMAC-SHA256 can compete. The starter kits simply eliminate boilerplate for the most common choices.

issue.notes:
## Focus-Fire Phase Analysis Complete

### Overview
The focus-fire combat phase (engine/turn.go:201-290) implements a simultaneous, comparison-based combat resolution algorithm. Unlike traditional HP/attack systems, bots die based on relative threat density.

### Core Algorithm (3 phases)

**Phase 1: Count Enemies in Range (lines 204-223)**
- For each alive bot, count enemies within AttackRadius2
- Uses Grid.InRadius() with toroidal distance (grid.go:114-115)
- Stores counts in enemyCounts map and enemy references in botsInRadius map
- AttackRadius2 default: 12 (sqrt(12) ≈ 3.46 tiles) - see types.go:192

**Phase 2: Determine Deaths Simultaneously (lines 225-248)**
- Uses pre-computed enemyCounts (no cascading deaths within same phase)
- For each bot with enemies in range:
  - Check if myEnemyCount >= theirEnemyCount for ANY enemy
  - If true → bot marked dead
- Death condition: `myEnemyCount >= theirEnemyCount` creates 'outnumbered = death'

**Phase 3: Process Deaths and Events (lines 250-289)**
- Mark bots as dead, decrement player bot counts
- All enemies within attack radius are recorded as 'killers'
- Awards KillScore (default: 1) to ALL killers (multiple killers get credit)
- Emits EventCombatDeath with bot_id, owner, position, killers array

### Key Design Characteristics

**No Target Selection**
- Bots do not choose targets
- All enemies within attack radius automatically engage
- No focus-fire priority or targeting logic

**Binary Damage Model**
- No HP, damage accumulation, or overkill tracking
- Alive or dead (binary state)
- Death based solely on relative enemy count comparison

**Simultaneous Resolution**
- All combat decisions use pre-computed counts
- No 'death cascade' within phase
- Deaths processed after all decisions made

**Toroidal Distance Calculation (grid.go:78-95)**
- Grid wraps at edges
- Distance2 uses shortest path accounting for wrap
- Formula: takes shorter path around wrapped edge

### Relationship to Zone Shrink

**Zone Parameters (types.go:196-200)**
- ZoneEnabled: true
- ZoneStartTurn: 10 (zone activates, no shrink until turn 11)
- ZoneShrinkInterval: 1 (shrinks every turn after activation)
- ZoneShrinkStep: 1 tile per turn (matches bot movement speed)
- ZoneMinRadius: 1 tile (3+ player)

**Combat Convergence**
- Zone starts at 90% of distance from center to edge (turn.go:193)
- Shrinks 1 tile/turn starting turn 11
- Bots outside zone killed immediately (turn.go:152-155)
- Forces inward movement → guaranteed contact → combat

### Edge Cases Identified

1. **Equal Enemy Counts (A=2, B=2)**: Both die in mutual destruction
2. **Asymmetric (A=3, B=1)**: A dies (outnumbered), B lives
3. **Zero Enemies**: Bot safe (skip check at line 234)
4. **Multiple Killers**: All engaged enemies get kill credit and score
5. **Zone Death Precedence**: executeZone() comes AFTER executeCombat() in ExecuteTurn() (turn.go:28-31), so zone deaths happen AFTER combat that turn

### Configuration References

- AttackRadius2: types.go:166, default: 12 (types.go:192)
- KillScore: types.go:182, default: 1 (types.go:201)
- Zone config: types.go:174-179, defaults: types.go:196-200

No file changes required - this was analysis/documentation only.
issue.title: Analyze focus-fire phase implementation in engine/turn.go

Root cause identified: Zone minimum radius too large for 2-player mode

## Root Cause (Option A): Zone minimum radius is too large

Current: ZoneMinRadius = 2 for 2-player (diameter = 4 tiles)
Expected: ZoneMinRadius = 1 for 2-player (diameter = 2 tiles)

## Supporting Evidence from Replay:

✓ Combat IS executing: Turn 13 shows combat_death events
✓ Bots ARE reaching same area: Positions (17,19) and (14,22), distance ≈ 4.2 tiles  
✓ Damage IS being dealt: 1v1 mutual destruction (both died)
✓ Zone IS shrinking: Radius 18→15 over turns 10-13

Critical finding: At turn 13 when combat occurred:
- Zone radius: 15 (diameter 30) - still very large
- Bot distance: 4.2 tiles (within 5-tile attack radius)  
- Combat happened because bots chose to move together, NOT because zone forced them

## Code Path Responsible:

File: engine/types.go, line 250
Function: ConfigForPlayers()  
Specific line: cfg.ZoneMinRadius = 2 // Per plan §3.7.1: 2-player min radius

Current config creates zone diameter 4 (radius 2), allowing bots to stay 4 tiles apart at opposite edges - barely within 5-tile attack radius.

## Recommended Fix:

Change cfg.ZoneMinRadius from 2 to 1 for 2-player mode (engine/types.go:250).

This creates zone diameter 2, matching 3+ player mode and forcing bots within attack radius (5 > 2).
